sources.title: World War II
sources.extract:
World War II, or the Second World War (1 September 1939 – 2 September 1945), was a global conflict between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers. Nearly all of the world's countries were involved, with many engaging in total war on an unprecedented scale. World War II was the deadliest conflict in history, causing the deaths of 60 to 75 million people, a majority of whom were civilians. Millions died as a result of massacres, starvation, disease, and genocides. After the Allied victory, Germany, Austria, Japan, and Korea were occupied, and German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes.
The causes of World War II included unresolved tensions in the aftermath of World War I and the rise of fascism in Europe and militarism in Japan. Key events preceding the war included Japan's invasion of Manchuria in 1931, the Spanish Civil War, the outbreak of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1937, and Germany's annexations of Austria and the Sudetenland.
World War II began on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany, under Adolf Hitler, invaded Poland, after which the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany. Poland was also invaded by the Soviet Union in mid-September, and was partitioned between the two states under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact. In 1940, the Soviet Union annexed the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania, while Germany conquered Norway, Denmark, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands. After the fall of France in June 1940, the war continued, mainly between Germany, now assisted by Fascist Italy, and the British Empire and British Commonwealth, with fighting in the Balkans, Mediterranean, Middle East, East Africa, the aerial Battle of Britain, the Blitz, and the naval Battle of the Atlantic. sources.title: History of the European Union
sources.extract:
The European Union is a geo-political entity, created in 1993, covering a large portion of the European continent. It is founded upon numerous treaties and has undergone expansions and secessions that have taken it from six member states to 27, a majority of the states in Europe.
Since the beginning of the institutionalised modern European integration in 1948, the development of the European Union has been based on a supranational foundation that would "make war unthinkable and materially impossible" and reinforce democracy amongst its members as laid out by Robert Schuman and other leaders in the Schuman Declaration (1950) and the Europe Declaration (1951). This principle was at the heart of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) (1951), the Treaty of Paris (1951), and later the Treaty of Rome (1957) which established the European Economic Community (EEC) and the European Atomic Energy Community (EAEC). The Maastricht Treaty (1992) created the European Union with its pillars system, including foreign and home affairs alongside the European Communities. This in turn led to the creation of the single European currency, the euro (launched 1999). The ECSC expired in 2002. The Maastricht Treaty has been amended by the treaties of Amsterdam (1997), Nice (2001) and Lisbon (2007), the latter merging the three pillars into a single legal entity, though the EAEC has maintained a distinct legal identity despite sharing members and institutions.

sources.title: Outline of World War II
sources.description: Overview of and topical guide to World War II
sources.extract:
The following outline is provided as an overview of and topical guide to World War II:
World War II, or the Second World War was a global military conflict that was fought between September 1, 1939, and September 2, 1945. The war pitted two major military alliances against each other: the Allies of the United States, Soviet Union, United Kingdom, China and others against the Axis of Germany, Japan, Italy and others. Over 60 million people, the majority of them civilians, were killed, making it the deadliest conflict in human history.
The Second World War was known for modern warfare and tactics such as air warfare, strategic bombing, blitzkrieg and the first, and only, use of nuclear weapons in warfare. It is also known for the numerous war crimes committed during its duration, mostly by Axis forces but also by Allied forces, that left tens of millions of civilians dead through genocides, massacres and starvation; such as the Holocaust, Three Alls Policy, Genocide of ethnic Poles, Unit 731, Nanjing massacre, Hunger Plan and the Warsaw Uprising.

page-1.text:
World War II, or the Second World War, was a global conflict fought between the Allies and the Axis powers from 1 September 1939 to 2 September 1945 [1]. It involved nearly all of the world's countries and was the deadliest conflict in history, causing 60 to 75 million deaths, most of them civilians, through massacres, starvation, disease, and genocide [1].

The war grew out of unresolved tensions after World War I, the rise of fascism in Europe, and militarism in Japan [1]. It began when Nazi Germany under Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, prompting the United Kingdom and France to declare war on Germany [1]. The Soviet Union also invaded Poland that month, and the two states partitioned the country under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact [1].

During the war, Germany conquered much of Western Europe, while the Soviet Union annexed the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania [1]. Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941, opening the Eastern Front [1]. After the Allied victory, Germany, Austria, Japan, and Korea were occupied, and German and Japanese leaders were tried for war crimes [1].

reports.title: World War II: Causes, Course, and Consequences, 1939–1945
reports.abstract: This report examines World War II from its origins to its legacy, establishing that the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression created instability exploited by Nazi Germany and other fascist powers[1][2]. It traces the war's outbreak with the German invasion of Poland in 1939 and its global expansion through campaigns in Europe, North Africa, and the Pacific[3][4]. The analysis covers the Axis and Allied strategies, the Holocaust and occupation policies, and the economic shift favoring the Allies[5][6][7]. Finally, it establishes that the war's end in 1945 produced the United Nations, the Cold War, decolonisation, and a transformed global order[8][9].
questions: What political, economic, and ideological factors caused the outbreak of World War II?
How did the major military campaigns and theatres shape the course and outcome of the war?
What were the roles, strategies, and perspectives of the principal belligerents, including the Axis and Allied powers?
What were the immediate and long-term consequences of the war for global politics, society, and international order?

answers.text: The outbreak of World War II was caused by the Treaty of Versailles, which imposed severe territorial, military, and financial penalties on Germany, fostering deep resentment[1]. The Great Depression intensified economic hardship and social unrest, helping fascist movements gain ground[2]. Nazi racial ideology and expansionist aims drove rearmament and aggression, while the appeasement policy of Britain and France, culminating in the Munich Agreement of 1938, failed to restrain Hitler[10].

The war began with Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, followed by declarations of war from Britain and France[3]. Global expansion included Japan's attacks in December 1941, with turning points at Midway and Stalingrad in 1942–43 shifting momentum[4]. The Allied invasions of Italy and Normandy in 1943–44, followed by the collapse of Germany and Japan in 1945, determined the war's outcome[3].

The Axis powers—Germany, Italy, and Japan—were bound by anti-Communism and dissatisfaction with the post-World War I order, pursuing expansion through the Mukden Incident, the invasion of Ethiopia, and aims for Lebensraum[5][11]. The Allies, comprising the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, United States, and China, combined British naval resources, Soviet manpower, American industrial support, and Chinese resistance[12][13]. The Allies' economic advantage grew from a 2.4:1 GDP ratio in 1938 to 5.0:1 by 1945, underpinning their victory[7].

Immediate consequences included Germany's unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945, the Potsdam settlement dividing Germany into occupation zones, and the founding of the United Nations in 1945[8][9]. Long-term effects encompassed the onset of the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, accelerated decolonisation across Asia and Africa, and territorial changes including the expulsion of Germans from Central and Eastern Europe[14].

parts.title: Origins and Causes of World War II
parts.focus: This part examines the political, economic, and ideological conditions that led to the outbreak of war in 1939.
parts.summary: This part establishes that the Treaty of Versailles imposed severe territorial, military, and financial penalties on Germany, creating deep resentment and instability that Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party exploited after coming to power in 1933. Economic hardship from the Great Depression intensified social unrest and helped fascist movements gain ground, while Nazi racial ideology and expansionist aims drove German rearmament and aggression. A policy of appeasement by Britain and France, culminating in the Munich Agreement of 1938, failed to restrain Hitler and paved the way for war in 1939.\n

sections.heading: The Treaty of Versailles and postwar instability
sections.text:
World War I radically altered the European political map, with the Central Powers losing territory and new nation-states created from the dissolved Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, and Russian empires[1][15]. The League of Nations was established in 1920 to prevent armed conflict through collective security and peaceful negotiation, but irredentist and revanchist nationalism emerged in several states, especially Germany[1]. The Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, stripped Germany of around 13 per cent of its home territory and all overseas possessions, limited its army to 100,000 men, demilitarised and occupied the Rhineland, and imposed reparations[1][10][16][17][15]. Germans viewed the terms as harsh and humiliating, and Nazi leader Adolf Hitler called the treaty a design to ruin the German nation; undoing it became a central tenet of the Nazi Party[16][17].

The Polish Corridor, created under Articles 27 and 28 of the treaty and effective from 20 January 1920, gave Poland access to the Baltic Sea from 70 per cent of the dissolved province of West Prussia, including about 140 km of coastline[18]. The broader postwar settlement redrew borders and produced a larger number of smaller powers, making the European balance of power less stable[15]. Historians note that the Versailles Treaty failed to establish a workable international system or lasting European integration[19].

After 1890, Kaiser Wilhelm II's Weltpolitik had increased German imperial ambitions, and fragile alliances helped trigger the First World War in 1914[20]. One objective of Versailles was to abolish the dominance of the balance-of-power concept and replace it with the League of Nations, though Austria and majority-German areas of the Czech lands were not permitted to join Germany[20].

sections.heading: The rise of Nazism and fascist ideology
sections.text:
Adolf Hitler became chancellor of Germany in 1933 after political maneuverings around the ageing President Paul von Hindenburg brought the Nazis to power on 30 January 1933[2][21]. The Nazis soon abolished parliamentary democracy, espoused a radical racist revision of the world order, and began a rearmament campaign[2]. After Hindenburg's death in 1934, Hitler proclaimed himself Führer and supreme commander of the armed forces, whose members swore an oath of loyalty to him personally[2].

The Great Depression caused international social unrest, and fascist propaganda blamed economic problems on minorities and scapegoats such as "Judeo-Masonic-bolshevik" conspiracies, left-wing internationalism, and immigrants[22]. In Germany, the Depression contributed to the rise of the Nazi Party, the demise of the Weimar Republic, and the establishment of a fascist regime with expansionist territorial aims[22]. From 1933, liberal democracy was dissolved and the Nazis mobilised the country for war, implementing racial laws that discriminated against, disenfranchised, and persecuted Jews and other minorities[22].

Fascist ideology drew on older roots, including admiration for ancient Sparta's militarism and racial purity and for ancient Rome's capacity to forge a strong, unified civilisation[23][24]. Hitler claimed Christianity had weakened Rome by authorising racial intermixing[23]. Early admirers of Mussolini's March on Rome included Hitler, who modelled the Nazi Party on the Italian Fascists; the failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich in November 1923 led to Hitler's arrest and detention until 1925[25].

sections.heading: German expansion and the failure of appeasement
sections.text:
In March 1938, Germany annexed Austria, provoking little response from other European powers[10]. Encouraged, Hitler pressed German claims on the Sudetenland, an area of Czechoslovakia with a predominantly ethnic German population[10]. In a speech at the Sportpalast in Berlin, he claimed the Sudetenland was "the last territorial demand I have to make in Europe" and set a deadline of 28 September 1938 at 2:00 p.m. for Czechoslovakia to cede it or face war[26].

Britain and France followed Neville Chamberlain's appeasement policy and conceded the Sudetenland to Germany in the Munich Agreement, made against the wishes of the Czechoslovak government, in exchange for a promise of no further territorial demands[10][26]. On 29 September 1938, Hitler, Daladier, and Chamberlain met in Munich and signed the agreement, accepting the immediate occupation of the Sudetenland; Czechoslovakia, not party to the talks, submitted to compulsion and promised to abide by it on 30 September[26]. Soon afterwards, Germany and Italy forced Czechoslovakia to cede additional territory to Hungary, and Poland annexed the Trans-Olza region[10].

Some historians argue that elites handed power to the Nazis at a moment when the party was close to disintegrating[27], while others emphasise the structural role of Versailles, the Depression, and the weakness of the League of Nations[1][19][16][17]. The appeasement period left Czechoslovakia dismembered and demonstrated that Britain and France would not resist German expansion by force.

parts.title: Major Theatres and Military Campaigns
parts.focus: This part covers the principal phases and battles across the European, Mediterranean, and Pacific theatres from 1939 to 1945.
parts.summary: This part establishes that World War II began with the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, followed by the Soviet invasion on 17 September under the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, and that Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. It outlines the subsequent global expansion of the conflict, including the Winter War, the German occupation of Denmark and Norway, Japan's attacks in December 1941, the turning points at Midway and Stalingrad in 1942–43, the Allied invasion of Italy, the Normandy landings in 1944, and the final collapse of Germany and Japan in 1945. The evidence also notes the brutal character of the invasion of Poland, including Nazi plans for annihilation and colonization.

sections.heading: Outbreak in Europe, 1939
sections.text: On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland after staging false flag border incidents, opening the war with an attack on the Polish defences at Westerplatte[3][28]. Britain and France responded with an ultimatum and declared war on Germany on 3 September after it was ignored[3][29]. The German assault combined air power and armor in mobile warfare later termed Blitzkrieg; Poland mobilized late, lacked modern arms and had few armored units, and its army was defeated within weeks despite inflicting serious German casualties[29]. On 17 September, two days after signing a cease-fire with Japan, the Soviet Union invaded Poland under the pretext that the Polish state had ceased to exist[30]. Warsaw surrendered on 27 September, and the last large operational Polish unit surrendered on 6 October[30]. Poland never surrendered formally; a government-in-exile and a clandestine state remained, and many Polish military personnel evacuated to Romania and Latvia to fight later against the Axis[30].

sections.heading: The Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact and Eastern Europe
sections.text: On 23 August 1939, Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact in Moscow, whose secret protocol divided eastern European border states into spheres of influence and provided for the partition of Poland[31][32]. The pact stunned the world given the parties' earlier mutual hostility and conflicting ideologies[31]. Its conclusion was followed by the German invasion of Poland on 1 September, which triggered the outbreak of war in Europe, and then the Soviet invasion of Poland, leading to the annexation of its eastern part[31]. Western Byelorussia was included in the BSSR, tens of thousands were imprisoned in Gulag camps, exiled or executed as enemies of the people, with victims mostly Polish and Jewish[33]. Finland, assigned to the Soviet sphere, refused Soviet demands and was attacked in November 1939, leading to the Winter War; the Soviet Union failed to annex Finland but received territory under the Moscow Peace Treaty in March 1940[32].

sections.heading: Scandinavia and the Phoney War
sections.text: During the Phoney War period, the alliance provided no direct military support to Poland outside a cautious French probe into the Saarland[3]. The Western Allies began a naval blockade of Germany aimed at damaging its economy and war effort[3]. Germany responded by ordering U-boat warfare against Allied merchant and warships, which later escalated into the Battle of the Atlantic[3]. The German occupation of Denmark and Norway from April 1940 severed practical Finnish connections to countries other than the Soviet Union, Nazi Germany and Sweden[32]. A proposed Swedish–Finnish military alliance failed due to Soviet–German pressure[32].

sections.heading: Global Expansion and Allied Victory, 1941–1945
sections.text: In December 1941, Japan attacked American and British territories in Asia and the Pacific, including Pearl Harbor in Hawaii, leading the United States to enter the war against the Axis[34]. Japan conquered much of coastal China and Southeast Asia, but its Pacific advances were halted in June 1942 at the Battle of Midway[34]. In early 1943, Axis forces were defeated in North Africa and at Stalingrad in the Soviet Union[34]. An Allied invasion of Italy in July resulted in the fall of its fascist regime, and Allied offensives in the Pacific and the Soviet Union forced the Axis to retreat on all fronts[34]. In 1944, the Western Allies invaded France at Normandy, opening a new front, and the Soviet Union advanced into Central Europe[34]. Japan suffered major setbacks, including the crippling of its navy by the United States, the loss of key Western Pacific islands, and defeats in Burma[34]. The war in Europe concluded with the liberation of German-occupied territories and an invasion of Germany itself, culminating in the fall of Berlin and Germany's unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945[34].

parts.title: The Axis Powers: Germany, Italy, and Japan
parts.focus: This part explores the aims, leadership, military strategies, and collaboration of the principal Axis belligerents.
parts.summary: This part establishes the Axis powers as Germany, Italy, and Japan, bound by anti-Communism and dissatisfaction with the post-World War I order. It traces Mussolini's rise to power in 1922, Italy's expansionist wars in Ethiopia and Albania, and Japan's aggression from the 1931 Mukden Incident through the 1937 invasion of China. It also outlines German aims for Lebensraum in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union under Adolf Hitler, and notes the shifting Axis strategies, including Japan's turn southward after 1939 and Italy's entry into the war in 1940 followed by surrender in 1943.

sections.heading: Fascist Italy and Its Imperial Ambitions
sections.text: Benito Mussolini seized power as Prime Minister of Italy in 1922 after the March on Rome, in which Blackshirts converged on the capital while King Victor Emmanuel III declined to risk bloodshed by dispersing them[37]. Initially heading a coalition government with only three Fascist ministers among fourteen, Mussolini consolidated control through the Grand Council of Fascism and pursued economically liberal policies at first before moving toward a totalitarian, nationalist state[38]. Italian Fascism sought to complete the Risorgimento by incorporating Italia Irredenta, claiming Dalmatia, Malta, Corfu, Italian Switzerland, Corsica, Nice, and Savoy[39]. Mussolini invaded Ethiopia in 1935, founded Italian East Africa, and withdrew Italy from the League of Nations amid international isolation[5]. Italy annexed Albania in 1939 and entered the war on Germany's side in 1940, only to be forced to surrender to the Allies in September 1943[39][5].

sections.heading: Nazi Germany's Aims and Leadership
sections.text: Under dictator Adolf Hitler, Nazi Germany aimed to acquire a vast empire of living space (Lebensraum) in eastern Europe and the Soviet Union, calculating that German hegemony in Europe would require war[40]. The regime had begun planning a European war from the day the Nazis came to power in late January 1933[40]. Germany incorporated Austria and the Czech lands without war in 1938 and 1939, then secured Soviet neutrality through a non-aggression pact[40]. The Axis partnership, comprising Nazi Germany, Imperial Japan, and Fascist Italy, was based on anti-Communism and dissatisfaction with the world order after World War I, with the intention of establishing permanent dominance over Europe and Asia respectively through military conquest[40].

sections.heading: Japan's Expansion and Strategic Shift
sections.text: Japanese aggression in Asia began with the Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, an autonomous decision by Kwantung Army leadership that began the period sometimes called the Fifteen Years War[11]. Japan established the puppet state of Manchukuo in February 1932, nominally headed by the dethroned emperor Puyi, and left the League of Nations in February 1933 after the Lytton Report blamed Japan for the conflict[41]. In July 1937, Japan captured Peking after the Marco Polo Bridge incident and launched a campaign to invade all of China, taking Shanghai after three months of fighting and capturing Nanking in December 1937[4]. In the mid-to-late 1930s, the Imperial Army favoured northern expansion under Hokushin-ron, but defeat at Khalkin Gol in 1939, the ongoing war in China, and the German-Soviet neutrality pact made this difficult; Japan signed a Neutrality Pact with the Soviet Union in April 1941 and adopted the Navy's southern strategy, Nanshin-ron, which led to war with the United States and Western Allies[42].

sections.heading: Axis Collaboration and Military Alignment
sections.text: Italy allied with Nazi Germany and the Empire of Japan and strongly supported Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War[5]. The Axis powers were the most significant members of a partnership founded on anti-Communism and shared grievances over the post-World War I order[40]. Germany, Italy, and Japan pursued coordinated but distinct expansionist goals: German hegemony in eastern Europe, a New Roman Empire in the Mediterranean and Africa, and Japanese dominance in Asia[40][5][39]. The main Axis leaders were Adolf Hitler, Hirohito, and Benito Mussolini[43].

parts.title: The Allied Powers: United Kingdom, Soviet Union, United States, and China
parts.focus: This part examines the alliance, contributions, and strategic perspectives of the major Allied nations.
parts.summary: This part establishes that the United Kingdom, Soviet Union, United States, and China formed the core of the Allied Powers, with Churchill leading British resistance after the fall of France and Stalin joining the Allies following Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. The alliance combined British naval and imperial resources, Soviet manpower on the Eastern Front, American industrial and material support, and Chinese resistance against Japan, creating an economic advantage over the Axis that grew from a 2.4:1 GDP ratio in 1938 to 5.0:1 by 1945. The evidence also shows that Finland's complex position—fighting the Soviet Union twice while later aligning with the Allies against Germany—illustrates the shifting alignments of the wider conflict, though Finland itself is not one of the four principal Allied powers examined here.

sections.heading: The United Kingdom under Churchill
sections.text: After Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, the United Kingdom and France declared war on Germany[12]. Following the fall of France in June 1940, the war continued mainly between Germany, assisted by Fascist Italy, and the British Empire and British Commonwealth, with fighting across multiple theatres including the Battle of Britain, the Blitz, and the Battle of the Atlantic[12]. Churchill rallied the nation in defiance of Hitler, and his wartime speeches were described as among the most powerful ever given in the English language, reaching out to everyone in Britain, across Nazi-occupied Europe, and throughout the world[45]. Churchill understood from the very start that Britain could not win without the eventual participation of the United States, and he conducted a relentless campaign to persuade President Franklin Roosevelt to come to the defence of embattled Britain[46]. After six years of war, the British people rejected Churchill and the Conservatives on 26 July 1945, and Labour under Clement Attlee took power[45]. Churchill later used his six-volume memoir series to create an Anglocentric interpretation of the war, justifying his decisions and shaping how the struggle was remembered[47].

sections.heading: The Soviet Union Enters the Alliance
sections.text: The Soviet Union had initially been aligned with Germany through the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, invading Poland from the east in mid-September 1939 and partitioning Poland with Germany[12]. The USSR then annexed the Baltic states and parts of Finland and Romania in 1940[12], and invaded Finland on 30 November 1939, starting the Winter War, which ended on 13 March 1940 with Finland ceding 9% of its territory[48]. This dynamic changed decisively on 22 June 1941, when Germany and several European Axis allies launched Operation Barbarossa, invading the western Soviet Union along a 2,900-kilometre front with more than 3.8 million Axis troops[13]. The operation opened the Eastern Front—the largest and deadliest land war in history—and brought the Soviet Union into the Allied powers[13]. The attack became the largest and costliest military offensive in human history, with around 10 million combatants in the opening phase and over 8 million casualties by the end of the operation on 5 December 1941[13].

sections.heading: The United States and China
sections.text: The evidence identifies Franklin D. Roosevelt as a main Allied leader alongside Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill, and Chiang Kai-shek[43], but the provided sources do not contain specific details about when the United States entered the war, the nature of American material aid, or the particular course of the American contribution. Similarly, Chiang Kai-shek is named as a principal Allied leader representing China[43], yet the evidence offers no information about China's role in the war, its resistance to Japan, or its strategic position within the alliance. The infobox also names Joseph Stalin, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Chiang Kai-shek as the main Allied leaders[43], confirming the four-power structure of the Allied direction even where the documentary record in this evidence is sparse.

sections.heading: Allied Economic and Material Advantage
sections.text: Chart evidence shows the Allies to Axis GDP ratio throughout the war, with values of 2.4 in 1938, 2.1 in 1939, 1.6 in 1940, 1.8 in 1941, 2.0 in 1942, 2.3 in 1943, 2.9 in 1944, and 5.0 in 1945[7]. The ratio dipped to its lowest point in 1940 at 1.6, reflecting the period when Germany dominated continental Europe and Britain stood largely alone, before rising steadily as the Soviet Union and the United States mobilised their economies for total war[7]. By 1945 the Allied economic advantage reached 5.0 to 1, underscoring the cumulative weight of American industrial production, Soviet wartime output, British imperial resources, and Chinese resistance against Japan[7]. This material superiority underpinned the Allied strategy of out-producing and out-lasting the Axis powers across all theatres.

parts.title: Key Themes: The Holocaust, Occupation, and Total War
parts.focus: This part addresses genocide, civilian experience, resistance, and the mobilization of societies and economies for war.
parts.summary: This part establishes that the Holocaust was a deliberate, systematic genocide in which nearly 6 million European Jews were murdered, alongside other targeted groups such as Roma, disabled people, homosexuals, Jehovah's Witnesses, and political dissidents. It shows how German occupation enabled mass murder through ghettos, deportations to killing centers like Auschwitz-Birkenau, and the participation of German military and police units in the Soviet Union. The evidence also indicates civilian life under occupation involved persecution, collaboration, resistance, and shifting social roles, though much of the remaining material concerns film genres rather than direct wartime experience.

sections.heading: The Holocaust and Nazi Occupation
sections.text: The Holocaust was a deliberate and systematic extermination of European Jews during World War II, carried out at numerous concentration camps as the Allied Powers fought Nazi Germany's domination of Europe[6]. Nearly 6 million Jews were murdered in this genocide[6]. Beyond Jews, the Nazis targeted the handicapped, mentally ill, Roma, Jehovah's Witnesses, homosexuals, and political dissidents for destruction[6]. With the start of the war and swift German victories, the Nazi regime pursued territorial expansion and racial goals under conditions of war and military occupation[49]. The German Army, SS, and German police units took an active part in authorized mass murders of Jews in the Soviet Union[49]. Germans and collaborators deported roughly 2.7 million Jews and others from occupied Europe to killing centers in German-occupied Poland, with Auschwitz-Birkenau receiving transports from across Europe[49]. Across eastern Europe, German authorities forced Jews into tightly packed ghettos separated from the non-Jewish population by brick walls and barbed wire[49]. The German drive eastward was cast as a crusade against Judaism and Communism[49].

sections.heading: Civilian Life, Resistance, and Collaboration
sections.text: In the Vardar Banovina, occupied between 1941 and 1944 by Italian-ruled Albania and pro-German Bulgaria, inhabitants who opposed the regime were persecuted, prompting some, including future first president Kiro Gligorov, to join Josip Broz Tito's Communist resistance movement[50]. The Bulgarian army was initially well received by much of the population and recruited locally, with locals forming as much as 40% to 60% of soldiers in certain battalions[50]. The Macedonian resistance received support from the Albanian National Liberation Movement and participated in battles such as the Kičevo Clashes, which led to the first town in Macedonia being liberated by partisans[50]. The Holocaust resulted from factors including historic antisemitism, eugenics, nationalism, the aftermath of the First World War, the rise of the Nazis, Adolf Hitler's role, the internal operation of the Nazi state, the Second World War, and collaboration[51]. The war radicalized Nazi antisemitic policy into genocide[51].

sections.heading: Total War and Mobilization on the Home Front
sections.text: Women's experience of total war included new economic and social roles. In the United States, collegiate men were drafted for World War II in the 1940s, creating opportunities for women to become cheerleaders on sporting event sidelines for the first time[52]. Women were believed to comprise a majority of movie-goers, giving the film industry an economic interest in producing prestigious woman's films that attracted top stars and directors[53]. The woman's film genre reached its zenith during World War II[53]. In the 1950s, many women who had been in the workforce during World War II faced the transition back into the home[54]. These shifts illustrate how total war mobilized societies and economies, altering gender roles even as the genre's critical reception remained contested between scholars who saw it as well-regarded and those who viewed the term as derogatory[53].

parts.title: Consequences and Legacy of World War II
parts.focus: This part analyzes the war's human and territorial costs, the onset of the Cold War, decolonization, and the creation of the United Nations.
parts.summary: This part establishes that World War II ended in 1945 with Germany’s unconditional surrender and the Potsdam settlement, which divided Germany into occupation zones and set the stage for the Cold War rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union. The United Nations was created in 1945 with China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States as permanent Security Council members, while Europe’s devastated great powers lost influence and decolonisation accelerated across Asia and Africa. Territorial changes included the flight and expulsion of Germans from Central and Eastern Europe and the degermanisation of those regions, alongside French colonial losses in Indochina and Algeria and the independence of India, Pakistan, and later Bangladesh. The war transformed global political, economic, and social structures, laying the foundation for international relations through the 20th and 21st centuries.

sections.heading: Wartime Conferences and the Postwar Settlement
sections.text: The Allied powers coordinated their strategy and postwar planning through a series of major conferences. At Tehran in 1943 and Moscow in 1943, the Three Allied Powers discussed plans for joint institutions in a postwar world, leading to the decision at Yalta in February 1945 to include Free France as the Fourth Allied Power and to form a European Advisory Commission, later replaced by the Council of Foreign Ministers and the Allied Control Council following the German surrender and the Potsdam Agreement in 1945[55][56]. The Yalta Conference, held on the Crimean coast between 4 and 11 February 1945, focused on the reorganisation of Europe after the war, including Germany’s unconditional surrender, division into zones of occupation, denazification, punishment of war criminals, German reparations, and the shape of the future international organisation that would become the United Nations[14]. Historians regard Yalta as controversial because of the compromises reached, particularly relating to eastern Europe, and it is described as where the first shivers of the Cold War were felt as the alliance between democracy and communism began to give way to rivalry and hostility[57][14]. The Potsdam Conference, held between 17 July and 2 August 1945 to the southwest of Berlin after Germany’s unconditional surrender on 8 May 1945, brought together Stalin, Truman, and Attlee (who replaced Churchill during the talks) to craft the final document dividing Germany and ensuring it would not pose a future military threat[57][14][8].

sections.heading: The United Nations and the Onset of the Cold War
sections.text: The United Nations was created to foster international cooperation and prevent future conflicts, with the victorious great powers—China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—becoming the permanent members of its Security Council[9]. The Soviet Union and the United States emerged as rival superpowers, setting the stage for the Cold War, a conflict between an American-led coalition and the Soviet/communist presence that dominated much of Eurasia[58][9]. UNESCO, the UN’s educational, scientific, and cultural branch, was also founded in 1945 as heir to the League’s International Committee on Intellectual Cooperation, though both the UN and UNESCO were at first hindered by the Cold War[59]. The foundation of the OECD in 1948 began to integrate Europe’s colonial realm, and the Hague Congress of 1948 laid the foundation of the Council of Europe in 1949[60].

sections.heading: Territorial Change, Expulsion, and Decolonisation
sections.text: In the wake of Europe’s devastation, the influence of its great powers waned, triggering the decolonisation of Africa and Asia[9]. Since the flight and expulsion of Germans from Central and Eastern Europe at the end of and after World War II, those territories have been mostly degermanised[61]. With the end of the war in 1945 and the ruination of Europe and imperial Japan, many countries in Asia rapidly freed themselves of colonial rule; Indian independence was accompanied by the carving out of Pakistan for South Asian Muslims, which in 1971 split into Pakistan and Bangladesh[62]. France slowly recovered after liberation in 1944 and enjoyed a baby boom, but long wars in Indochina and Algeria drained French resources and ended in political defeat; into the 1960s most of the French colonial empire became independent[63]. The failure of Britain and France in the Suez Crisis of 1956 was a major shock to the strongest remaining European colonial powers[60]. Many former colonies in the Pacific also became independent states after the war[64].

sections.heading: Global Transformation and Legacy
sections.text: World War II transformed the political, economic, and social structures of the world and established the foundation of international relations for the rest of the 20th century and into the 21st century[9]. Many countries whose industries had been damaged moved towards economic recovery and expansion[9]. The end of the Cold War in 1991 saw the emergence of several independent states from the former Soviet Union in East Europe and Central Asia, and the independence of the five modern Central Asian countries[58][62]. The last world war saw the irrecoverable destruction of national heritages and the terrible misuse of science, while the United Nations and UNESCO were founded in 1945 to do a better job at peace-keeping and cooperation[59].
